LEARN: HTTP

Hypertext Transport Protocol, HTTP, is an application-layer protocol responsible for retrieving and sending web pages. Http gives the world wide web the ability to view/host website content regardless of the location of the request. Without it, websites cannot exist as we know them today.

By default, http operates on port 80 via TCP for both client requests and server responses.

Commonly, http requests are made by a web browser. The request reaches the website's frontend (via routers and switches), which may be an internet-hosted web server or a corporation's server bank. Multiple servers can work together to handle process volume and speed up response time.

Multi-server website hosts are called web farms and are composed of three main server types:

  • Frontend server: A server hosting the website's content files such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.
  • Backend server: A server dedicated to application-specific tasks such as database API access and dynamic content rendering.
  • Database server: A server containing customer or sensitive data for the website in secure database tables.

Http traverses the web in network packet containers, called frames, via HTTP/2. HTTP/3 was published 06-06-2023 by the IETF.1

Frames
An independent chunk of data sent over a network.
Hypertext Transport Protocol
The data transfer protocol used on the World Wide Web.
Hypertext Transport Protocol/2
Emplaces http in frames for reduced latency.
Hypertext Transport Protocol/3
The third major version of http using QUIC, a multiplexed transport protocol built on UDP.1
Server
A computer dedicated to running programs that provide services to other programs or devices, either in the same computer or over a computer network.
Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)
Ensures reliable data exchange between devices.
Web Browser
A software application that allows a user to access and view websites on the World Wide Web.
Web Farm
Computing a large website that uses two or more servers to handle user requests.
Website
A collection of interlinked web pages on the World Wide Web that are typically accessible from the same base URL and reside on the same server.
